inclusion.GLOBAL_I1: Sample- The analysis must be on healthy adult participants (alone, or a healthy/control subgroup reported separately from clinical or special groups).
inclusion.GLOBAL_I2: Whole-brain evidence- The analysis must come from a group-level, univariate whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical map, such as a main effect or a within-group contrast.
inclusion.GLOBAL_I3: Judge the analysis, not the paper- decide from THIS analysis's name, description and table caption. That the paper is broadly social is not by itself a reason to assign a construct. You do NOT, however, need the contrast to isolate a construct in a pure or exclusive way- a contrast that engages a construct as part of a richer social task still counts.
inclusion.GLOBAL_I4: How to read a sparse label- an empty or generic analysis name (e.g. "analysis_0") usually means the analysis is the only one in its table, so the caption describes it fully. Judge from the caption and surrounding full text. A blank or uninformative name is never itself a reason to exclude.
inclusion.GLOBAL_I5: Assign every construct that applies, not just the best one- this benchmark's contrasts carry on average 1.34 construct labels each, and roughly 29% carry exactly two. After choosing the construct that fits best, explicitly check each of the other three and add any that the contrast also engages. Common genuine pairings, in descending frequency- perception_self with perception_others; social_communication with perception_others; affiliation_attachment with social_communication; social_communication with perception_self; affiliation_attachment with perception_others. Assign AT MOST two of the four constructs- no contrast in this benchmark required three or more.

exclusion.GLOBAL_E2: Seed-based connectivity, effective connectivity (e.g. PPI, DCM) or resting-state analyses (e.g. ICA, PLE, Hurst exponents), unless a separate qualifying univariate task-evoked map is explicitly the analyzed row.
exclusion.GLOBAL_E3: Contrasts between two GROUPS OF PARTICIPANTS (e.g. patients vs controls, men vs women, high- vs low-trait groups) or a group x condition interaction. This is about who is being compared, NOT about what is depicted- a within-subject contrast between social targets or conditions (self vs other, close other vs stranger, partner vs stranger, friend vs celebrity) is eligible and is in fact the standard design in this literature.

inclusion.SOCIAL_PROCESSING_ALL_I1: The analysis comes from a task involving social stimuli, social judgements or social interaction- this includes faces and facial expressions, voices and speech directed at or between people, gaze, gesture and imitation, self- and other-referential judgement, mentalizing and empathy, biological motion and action observation, and social exchange or bonding paradigms.
inclusion.SOCIAL_PROCESSING_ALL_I2: The contrast reflects some aspect of that social task rather than a purely perceptual, motor or physiological control effect.

inclusion.AFFILIATION_ATTACHMENT_I1: The contrast engages social bonding, closeness, affiliative value or relationship relevance. Task families the source paper places here- cooperation versus competition tasks; kinship or affiliative scenarios (situations involving mother, father, spouse or offspring versus non-affiliative or neutral ones); social comparison tasks (describing a close other such as a romantic partner versus a non-close other such as a roommate); perspective-taking toward a loved one versus a stranger; social acceptance or rejection by a specific person; and economic exchange where the relationship to the other player is the manipulated variable (e.g. dividing money between oneself and people who previously included or excluded one).
inclusion.AFFILIATION_ATTACHMENT_I2: Relationship closeness or affiliative value must be part of what the contrast varies- not merely that another person is present.

exclusion.AFFILIATION_ATTACHMENT_E1: Contrasts about deception or aggression where no bond, closeness or relationship dimension is manipulated. Note that competition and social-exchange paradigms are NOT excluded here- the source paper places cooperation-versus-competition and money-division tasks within this construct.

inclusion.SOCIAL_COMMUNICATION_I1: The contrast involves a communicative social signal, whether the participant is receiving or producing it. Task families the source paper places here- viewing pictures of faces (including face versus object or face versus non-face contrasts); emotional expression tasks such as judging happy, sad, angry or neutral faces; auditory social stimuli such as communicative versus non-communicative sounds, speech and prosody; direct versus averted gaze; and observing or mimicking hand movements and gestures.
inclusion.SOCIAL_COMMUNICATION_I2: Simple face viewing and facial-expression contrasts DO qualify. The source paper's most common Social Communication task is viewing pictures of faces, so do not require an explicit communicative-intent manipulation on top of the facial signal.

inclusion.PERCEPTION_SELF_I1: The contrast engages self-referential processing, self-knowledge, self-evaluation, agency or the bodily self. Task families the source paper places here- self versus other contrasts; self-judgements about personality-trait words ("does this adjective describe you?"); rating one's own emotional reaction to a stimulus; judging whether a picture or social role personally relates to oneself; imagining an event happening to oneself; viewing pictures of oneself; endorsing another's evaluation of oneself; and affective or social touch delivered to the participant (e.g. gentle brush strokes to the arm or palm).
inclusion.PERCEPTION_SELF_I2: The self side of a self-versus-other contrast is sufficient- the contrast does not need to be exclusively about the self. Note that self-versus-other is a within-subject condition contrast, not a between-group contrast.

inclusion.PERCEPTION_OTHERS_I1: The contrast engages perceiving, representing or reasoning about another person. Task families the source paper places here- Theory of Mind and mental-state inference (including inferring the mental states of characters in a film); empathy tasks; compassion ratings; judging another person's traits; observing an action being performed by another; imitation; and point-light biological motion (e.g. a coherent versus a scrambled walker).
inclusion.PERCEPTION_OTHERS_I2: Explicit mentalizing is NOT required. Action observation, imitation and biological motion qualify on the source paper's own accounting even though no mental-state inference is demanded of the participant.

exclusion.PERCEPTION_OTHERS_E1: Contrasts about object identity, or about the physical properties of a stimulus, where no other person is represented at all.
